raw_case_text: A 34-year-old Chinese male visited his local tertiary hospital due to progressively worsening occipital headache for the past 4 days, without showing any other symptoms of fever, projectile vomiting and so on. His medical history showed that he had had cryptococcal meningitis and HIV infection for about 1 year, and he had been receiving (with good compliance) fluconazole and tenofovir-lamivudine-dolutegravir based antiretroviral therapy (ART) during the same time period. The levels of the inflammatory markers were normal (Leukocytes 5.61*109 cells/mL, C-reactive protein 7 mg/dL). His neurological signs showed no abnormal indications. Head Computed Tomography (CT) scan revealed no abnormalities. The lumber puncture was performed and the test result of CSF is shown in Table 1. It shows rising levels of OP, lymphocytes and protein in CSF. The cryptococcus capsular antigen test result of CSF was positive but the results for the gram staining and culture study were negative. The patient was diagnosed with cryptococcal meningitis and was given fluconazole (400 mg, QD) continuously and TMP-SMX (0.48, QD) for 1 week by the doctor at the local hospital. However, his headache problem was not resolved. Then he came to our institution, the Infectious Disease Department of the First Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Zhejiang University, and was hospitalized. Upon arrival, the patient's body temperature was 36.7 C, pulse rate was 95 beats/min, blood pressure was 138/97 mmHg, respiratory rate was 23 breaths/min, and finger pulse SpO2 was 98%. He was suffering from headache but his neurological signs were normal. The laboratory results are as follows: white blood cell count 7.0 x 109/L, with a neutrophil ratio of 42%, hemoglobin 150 g/L, and platelet count 294 x 109/L; C-reactive protein (CRP)1.8 mg/L; CD4 count 171 cells/muL; normal blood biochemical; negative 1,3-beta-D-glucan test (G test) and galactomannan test (GM test) results (0.1 mug/L). The IgG antibodies of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and Human Cytomegalovirus (CMV) were positive, while the IgM antibodies and the test of the nucleic acid of EBV and CMV were negative. The test result for mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) was negative based on the blood test with T-SPOT, and the result for cryptococcus capsular antigen test of the blood was positive. The chest CT scan and echocardiography results were normal. The lumber puncture was performed on day 2 and the opening pressure was 285 (cm H2O). The test result of CSF is shown in Table 1. The cryptococcus capsular antigen test of CSF was positive. An India Ink microscopy on the CSF sample for cryptococcus was also performed and the result was negative. The results of the blood and CSF smears of bacteria and fungi were negative. The results of the acid-fast staining of CSF smear and GeneXpert were both negative for MTB. The test of the nucleic acid of CMV and EBV in CSF was negative. Based on the negative gram staining and culture study results of CSF provided by the local hospital and the above results, the CSF sample was sent to the laboratory for conventional tests and NGS test (using the Illumina Platform, IngeniGen. Ltd, Zhejiang, China) for pathogen-induced meningitis verification. Contrast-enhanced and diffusion-weighted MRI (3.0T) was performed on day 3, and the partial cerebellar surface enhancement was revealed (Figure 1), which matched the manifestation of cryptococcal meningitis, and no abnormal signals were detected in the cerebral parenchyma. Two days later, the NGS results showed that streptococcus suis (6 reads) and streptococcus mitis (1 reads) were found in CSF. The results of the blood and CSF culture of bacteria and fungi were still negative on day 5. So, we inquired the patient's medical history again, and he told us he had had close contact with a truck transporting pigs and had choked on water in a water park 2 weeks before his admission. Based on the test reports and his contact history, the diagnosis of streptococcus suis infection was made and intravenous Ceftriaxone (2.0, QD) was given. The patient's headache problem was resolved gradually. A second lumber puncture performed on day 12 revealed improved conditions of CSF (see Table 1), with negative gram staining and culture study results. Ceftriaxone was given to the patient for another 2 weeks and then oral moxifloxacin (0.4, QD) for 2 days. The third lumber puncture was performed on day 17, showing continuous conditional improvement of CSF. The patient was discharged in stable condition on day 21 after 1 week of receiving moxifloxacin. Three weeks later, we performed the fourth lumber puncture to confirm that the meningitis infection was cleared, but the patient's OP level was still abnormal, so fluconazole was given continuously until the OP level and cryptococcus capsular antigen test turned normal 6 months later.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old male presenting with progressively worsening occipital headache for four days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 4-day history of worsening occipital headache without accompanying fever, neck stiffness, or projectile vomiting. He had been managed at a local tertiary facility with fluconazole and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for one week without symptom relief. Two weeks prior to hospital admission, he had occupational contact with a pig transport truck and experienced an episode of water aspiration at a water park.
subjective.past_medical_history: Receiving compliant combination antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, lamivudine, and dolutegravir) and secondary antifungal prophylaxis with fluconazole for treated cryptococcal meningitis diagnosed one year earlier. Epidemiological exposure: Direct contact with a truck transporting pigs and water aspiration at a water park two weeks prior to admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Persistent occipital headache; denies fever, projectile vomiting, photophobia, altered mentation, or focal neurological deficits.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature 36.7 °C, heart rate 95 beats/min, blood pressure 138/97 mmHg, respiratory rate 23 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air. Neurological examination: Fully conscious, oriented, cranial nerves intact, meningeal signs absent, no focal neurological deficits.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: White blood cell count 7.0 x 10^9/L (42% neutrophils), hemoglobin 150 g/L, platelet count 294 x 10^9/L. Biochemistry: Normal serum electrolytes, renal function, and liver enzymes. Inflammatory markers: C-reactive protein 1.8 mg/L (7 mg/dL at initial evaluation). Fungal serologies: 1,3-beta-D-glucan (G-test) and galactomannan (GM-test, 0.1 microg/L) negative. Mycobacterial screening: T-SPOT.TB negative. Viral serologies: EBV IgG and CMV IgG positive, with negative IgM and negative viral DNA PCR. Echocardiogram: Normal. Chest CT: Normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI (3.0T, contrast-enhanced and diffusion-weighted): Partial cerebellar surface leptomeningeal enhancement compatible with prior cryptococcal meningitis; no focal parenchymal lesions or abnormal signal intensities. Serial lumbar punctures: Day 2 opening pressure 285 mmH2O; CSF India ink microscopy, Gram stain, bacterial/fungal cultures, acid-fast stain, and GeneXpert MTB were negative; CSF CMV and EBV PCR negative; CSF and blood cryptococcal capsular antigen positive. Day 12 and Day 17 follow-up lumbar punctures demonstrated progressive clearance of pleocytosis and normalizing CSF protein.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Streptococcus suis meningitis superimposed on treated cryptococcal meningitis and underlying human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (CD4+ T-cell count 171 cells/microL). Diagnostic confirmation: Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS, Illumina platform) of CSF detected Streptococcus suis (6 specific sequence reads) and Streptococcus mitis (1 read), corroborated by epidemiologic exposure to swine transport. Persistent CSF cryptococcal antigen positivity was attributed to residual antigenemia from prior infection. Plan & Outcome: Treated with intravenous ceftriaxone 2.0 g daily for 3 weeks followed by oral moxifloxacin 0.4 g daily for 1 week. Occipital headache rapidly subsided, and serial CSF evaluations confirmed resolution of acute bacterial infection. Discharged on hospital day 21. Continued maintenance fluconazole therapy until CSF opening pressure and cryptococcal antigen titers normalized at 6 months.
